opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something right in the spirit of it. If you believe transformative AI might arrive very soon, then work that pays off quickly matters a lot, and people should ask themselves whether what they're doing will still be relevant if timelines turn out short. That's a healthy question.

But as general advice for everyone, it's far too narrow, for a few reasons.

The first is simply uncertainty about timelines. We don't know when the crucial period will be. There's real probability mass on things taking longer: ten years, twenty years, maybe more. If the whole field restricts itself to work that shows results within a year, we'd be systematically neglecting all the worlds where we have more time. Those worlds might be ones where we have a lot of leverage, because there's room for deeper work to mature. A portfolio approach makes much more sense. Some people should work on the urgent, near-term things, and others should be building foundations.

The second is that a lot of the most important work doesn't have demonstrable impact on that kind of timescale even when it's very valuable. Think about building institutions, shaping norms, developing governance frameworks, training up the next generation of researchers, or doing conceptual work that clarifies what the problem even is. Much of the intellectual groundwork in this field took years before it influenced anything, but it ended up shaping how a lot of people think. If you'd applied a twelve-month test at the time, you'd have said it wasn't worth doing.

The third is a measurement problem. "Demonstrable" tends to mean legible, and legible tends to mean the kind of impact that's easy to point to: a paper, a benchmark, a policy mention. Those things matter, but optimising hard for legibility can push people toward work that looks productive rather than work that actually reduces risk. Some of the most important contributions are things like preventing a bad decision or quietly improving the judgment of people in key positions, and those are very hard to demonstrate at all, let alone within a year.

And finally, there's the question of comparative advantage. People differ a lot. Someone early in their career might do far more good by spending a few years building skills and credibility than by rushing into whatever has a fast payoff. Telling everyone to optimise for the same short horizon throws away a lot of that diversity.

So I'd put it this way: take short timelines seriously, and let them shift your priorities somewhat. But don't let them collapse the whole field onto a single strategy. Humanity's response to this challenge is much more robust if we're hedging across different possible futures.

r001.rationale: The response says some people may spend years building skills and credibility, but does not say switching into AI policy is worthwhile or that those skills enable substantive work after a year.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I understand where that kind of advice comes from. There's a real sense of urgency around AI at the moment, and when you feel that urgency, it's natural to want to see results quickly. You want to know that what you're doing is actually making a difference, and twelve months feels like a reasonable horizon for checking that. So I don't think it's a crazy heuristic.

But I do think it's too restrictive, for a few reasons.

The first is just that a lot of the most important work doesn't look like it's having an impact within a year. If you think back over the history of this field, some of the foundational contributions — the early conceptual work on what the problem even is, the work on decision theory, the work on interpretability that took years before it produced anything you could point to — none of that would have passed a twelve-month impact test. And yet without it, we'd be in a much worse position now. So if everyone had followed that advice ten years ago, the field would be impoverished in ways that are now quite hard to see, because you don't see the counterfactual.

The second thing is that "demonstrable" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Demonstrable to whom? There's a real risk that this just collapses into "work that is legible to the people currently funding or evaluating the field". And those people are often very good, but they have particular views about what matters, and those views might be wrong. A healthy field needs some fraction of people pursuing lines that the mainstream doesn't yet recognise as promising. If you demand demonstrable impact on a short timescale, you're essentially selecting against anything that's genuinely new.

The third point is about uncertainty over timelines. The twelve-month framing implicitly assumes that we're in the endgame — that the key decisions are being made now and anything that pays off later is too late. And it might be that we're in the endgame. I take short timelines seriously. But I'm really not confident of it, and I don't think anyone should be. If there's a reasonable chance that the crucial period is five or ten or twenty years away, then you want a portfolio that includes work which only pays off on those horizons. Putting everything on the shortest timeline is a bet, and it's a bet I don't think the evidence supports making with the whole community's effort.

And I suppose there's a final, slightly more personal point, which is about what this does to people. If you tell everyone that their work has to be visibly useful within a year, you create a lot of anxiety and a lot of churn. People abandon things just as they're starting to get traction. They chase whatever is currently fashionable. And they burn out, because they're constantly having to justify themselves. Whereas some of the people who've done the most valuable work are people who were given room to think for a while without having to show their hand.

So I'd put it like this. The urgency is real, and some people absolutely should be doing work with a very short feedback loop — that's part of the portfolio. But it's one part. The advice as stated turns a reasonable component of a strategy into the whole strategy, and I think that's a mistake. What I'd rather say is: be honest with yourself about whether your work is on a path to mattering, keep checking that, but don't confuse "I can't demonstrate impact yet" with "this isn't worth doing".

r001.rationale: The response discusses long timelines and delayed impact generally, but does not say that switching into AI policy can be worthwhile when skill acquisition takes a year before substantive work begins.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s too restrictive because there are important kinds of work whose value you can’t demonstrate on that timescale. Foundational research is an obvious example. You might spend a year trying to get clearer about what the problem actually is, or developing a new approach, without producing something that measurably improves the safety of an existing system. And that could nevertheless turn out to be enormously valuable.

There’s also a distinction between having an impact and being able to demonstrate that you’ve had an impact. If we insist on the latter within 12 months, we’ll select for things that are easy to measure, which aren’t necessarily the things that matter most.

Now, I understand the motivation. You don’t want people working indefinitely on something with a very vague story about how it could help. It’s good to ask what success would look like and how your work could contribute. But that’s different from requiring everyone to produce a demonstrable result within a year. Even if you think AI timelines are quite short, there’s uncertainty about them, and we should have a portfolio of approaches. Some should be aimed at immediate problems, and some should be investments that take longer to pay off.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s too restrictive because there are important kinds of work where you shouldn’t expect to see the impact within 12 months. You might need to spend several years developing the expertise to make a contribution, or working through a fundamental question before you can show how it helps. If everyone has to demonstrate an impact each year, we could systematically neglect those opportunities.

There’s also a distinction between having an impact and being able to demonstrate it. Particularly with research, you can sometimes make progress that turns out to be very important, but whose importance wasn’t clear at the time. A requirement for demonstrable impact can push people towards things that are easy to measure rather than things that matter most.

That doesn’t mean we should give ourselves a blank cheque to work on anything indefinitely. We should be asking how our work could help, seeking criticism, and checking whether we’re making progress. But I’d want a portfolio that includes direct, near-term work alongside longer-term research and investment in people. Twelve months seems much too short as a universal constraint.
